opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't read too much into it. People sometimes look at our team and say, "Oh, a lot of PhDs, so you must be hiring for credentials." But that's not really how I think about it.

What I care about is whether someone has done real research before: whether they've sat with a hard problem for a long time, failed many times, and still had the curiosity to keep going. A PhD is one environment where people often get that kind of training, so it's natural that many of the people who fit end up having one. But the degree is a byproduct, not the criterion.

Some of the strongest people I've worked with were still students, or came straight from undergrad, or didn't follow a typical academic path at all. What they had in common was a kind of taste. They could tell which questions were worth asking. They had the patience to look at the data and the experiments themselves instead of just trusting a paper. And they weren't attached to their own ideas. If the experiment said they were wrong, they accepted it quickly.

In a field moving as fast as large models, a lot of what you learned even two or three years ago may already be outdated. So the signal I look for is less "what have you done" and more "how do you think, and how fast do you learn." If the share of PhDs on the team says anything, it's that we value people who enjoy research for its own sake. That matters more to me than the title on the diploma.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the PhD share signals that the team values people who enjoy research for its own sake, while describing the degree as a byproduct rather than a hiring criterion.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of the PhD share as a hiring target. It's an output, not an input. When we look at someone, what we're asking is whether they have real research taste and whether they can execute, meaning they can take a vague question and actually turn it into a clean experiment and a result. It happens that people who have spent years grinding through a PhD often have that, because they've been forced to find a problem, fail at it repeatedly, and still push through. So the share ends up high, but that's a consequence of what we select for, not a filter.

And I'd say the ratio tells you more about the stage of the work than about the people. In foundation model research right now, so much is still open. There isn't a textbook, there isn't a mature engineering playbook. You need people who are comfortable with that ambiguity, who can read a paper, form a hypothesis, and go test it without someone handing them a spec. That's a research temperament, and a PhD is one common place to build it.

But some of the strongest people I've worked with didn't have a doctorate. They had the same curiosity and the same discipline, just acquired differently. What I actually care about is whether someone is genuinely obsessed with the problem, whether they're honest about what works and what doesn't, and whether they can collaborate, because training large models is a team sport. If someone has that, I don't really care what their credentials look like.

r001.rationale: The response says the PhD share is an outcome of selecting for research ability and temperament, and that the ratio says more about the stage of the work than about the people. It does not clearly interpret the share as a signal of how strongly team members love research.
